Question 1: Implementing K-means

K-means is a relatively simple algorithm that we can write ourselves. For Questions 1 and 2, do not use an existing function that performs K-means directly.

Generate 10 observations with two independent standard normal coordinates. Set a random seed and report it. Randomly assign the observations to K=2K=2 clusters, making sure neither cluster is empty. Let C(i)C(i) denote the cluster assigned to observation xix_i, and let mkm_k denote the mean of cluster kk.

  1. Perform one iteration: calculate the cluster means, then assign each observation to its closest mean using Euclidean distance. Report the means and updated assignments, and plot the observations colored by their updated assignments.

  2. Write a function that repeats these two steps until the assignments stop changing or a specified maximum number of iterations is reached. Your function should work for a data matrix with any number of variables and a chosen number of clusters KK. Start from a nonempty assignment to each cluster; if a cluster becomes empty during iteration, keep its previous mean. Recalculate the cluster means from the final assignments before returning them. Return the final assignments, cluster means, and within-cluster sum of squares,

    ∑k=1K∑i:C(i)=k∥xi−mk∥2. \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i:\,C(i)=k}\lVert x_i-m_k\rVert^2.

  3. Apply your function to the same 10 observations from two different random initial assignments. Report the final plots, cluster means, and within-cluster sums of squares. Do the two runs produce the same grouping and objective value? Explain your findings.

Solution for Question 1

random_init <- function(n, K) {
  sample(c(seq_len(K), sample(K, n - K, replace = TRUE)))
}

cluster_means <- function(X, cl, K, prev = NULL) {
  M <- matrix(NA_real_, K, ncol(X))
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    idx <- which(cl == k)
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      M[k, ] <- colMeans(X[idx, , drop = FALSE])
    } else if (!is.null(prev)) {
      M[k, ] <- prev[k, ]
    }
  }
  M
}
assign_closest <- function(X, M) {
  n <- nrow(X); K <- nrow(M)
  D <- sapply(seq_len(K), function(k)
    rowSums((X - matrix(M[k, ], n, ncol(X), byrow = TRUE))^2))
  max.col(-D, ties.method = "first")
}

wcss <- function(X, cl, M) {
  sum((X - M[cl, , drop = FALSE])^2)
}

my_kmeans <- function(X, K, init = NULL, max_iter = 100) {
  X <- as.matrix(X)
  n <- nrow(X)
  cl <- if (is.null(init)) random_init(n, K) else init
  M <- cluster_means(X, cl, K)
  iters <- 0
  for (it in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    new_cl <- assign_closest(X, M)
    iters <- it
    if (all(new_cl == cl)) break          # assignments stopped changing
    cl <- new_cl
    M <- cluster_means(X, cl, K, prev = M)
  }
  M <- cluster_means(X, cl, K, prev = M)  # means consistent with final assignments
  list(cluster = cl, centers = M, wcss = wcss(X, cl, M), iter = iters)
}

Each loop pass is one “means then assignment” step. The loop stops when the assignment is unchanged, and the means are recomputed from the final assignments before returning, so they always match the returned clusters.

set.seed(1); initA <- random_init(10, 2)
set.seed(2); initB <- random_init(10, 2)
fitA <- my_kmeans(X, 2, init = initA)
fitB <- my_kmeans(X, 2, init = initB)

}

same_partition <- function(a, b) {
  nrow(unique(cbind(a, b))) == length(unique(a)) &&
    nrow(unique(cbind(a, b))) == length(unique(b))
}
same <- same_partition(fitA$cluster, fitB$cluster)

set.seed(3)
obj <- replicate(30, my_kmeans(X, 2)$wcss)
table(round(obj, 4))

5.7797 6.0028 10.637 
    21      7      2

The two runs end in different groupings with different objective values. K-means decreases the within-cluster sum of squares at every step, but the objective is non-convex, so the algorithm only reaches a local minimum that depends on the starting assignment. The 30 random starts above show how many distinct local optima occur for this data set. In practice one runs several random starts and keeps the solution with the smallest WCSS. Cluster labels are arbitrary, so the grouping (not the label numbers) is what should be compared.

Question 2: Image color compression

Pick your favorite color image and use your K-means function from Question 1 to cluster its pixels. For computational efficiency, resize the image to no more than 200×200200\times200 pixels and use its three RGB color channels.

  1. Plot the original image and report its dimensions. Transform it into a data matrix with one observation per pixel and three variables: red, green, and blue. Report the dimensions of this matrix.

  2. For K=2,3,5,10K=2,3,5,10, apply your function to the pixel data. Report the cluster means and within-cluster sum of squares for each KK. Reconstruct and plot each compressed image by replacing every pixel with its assigned cluster mean. Use the same RGB scale for all fits.

  3. Which value of KK would you choose for this image? Briefly justify your choice using the reconstructed images and the within-cluster sums of squares.

Solution for Question 2

img <- jpeg::readJPEG("data/image.jpg")
if (length(dim(img)) == 2) img <- array(img, c(dim(img), 3))  # grayscale -> 3 channels
img <- img[, , 1:3]

# Resize to at most 200 x 200 (nearest-neighbor subsampling, base R)
scale_f <- min(1, 200 / max(dim(img)[1:2]))
nh <- max(1, round(dim(img)[1] * scale_f)); nw <- max(1, round(dim(img)[2] * scale_f))
ri <- round(seq(1, dim(img)[1], length.out = nh))
ci <- round(seq(1, dim(img)[2], length.out = nw))
img <- img[ri, ci, , drop = FALSE]

show_img <- function(a, main = "") {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
  plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(0, dim(a)[2]), ylim = c(0, dim(a)[1]), asp = 1)
  rasterImage(a, 0, 0, dim(a)[2], dim(a)[1])
  title(main)
}
show_img(img, "Original image")
cat("Image dimensions (height x width x channels):", dim(img), "\n")

           B = as.vector(img[, , 3]))
cat("Pixel matrix dimensions:", dim(P), "\n")

  1. K-means for K = 2, 3, 5, 10
init_from_points <- function(X, K) {
  U <- unique(X)                                   
  if (nrow(U) < K) stop("Image has fewer than K distinct colors")
  seeds <- U[sample(nrow(U), K), , drop = FALSE]
  assign_closest(X, seeds)
}

Ks <- c(2, 3, 5, 10)
set.seed(2026)
fits <- lapply(Ks, function(K) my_kmeans(P, K, init = init_from_points(P, K), max_iter = 100))
names(fits) <- paste0("K=", Ks)

for (i in seq_along(Ks)) {
  cat("\n==== K =", Ks[i], "| WCSS =", round(fits[[i]]$wcss, 2),
      "| iterations =", fits[[i]]$iter, "====\n")
  print(round(fits[[i]]$centers, 3))
}

recon <- function(fit) {
  a <- array(fit$centers[fit$cluster, ], dim = c(h, w, 3))
  pmin(pmax(a, 0), 1)                       # same [0, 1] RGB scale for every fit
}

par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

wc <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "wcss")
data.frame(K = Ks, WCSS = round(wc, 2),
           pct_of_K2 = round(100 * wc / wc[1], 1))

     main = "WCSS vs. K")
  1. I would choose K = 5. The WCSS drops steeply from K = 2 to K = 5, and at K = 5 the reconstruction already keeps the main color regions of the image, whereas K = 2 and K = 3 merge distinct regions into flat blocks. Going from K = 5 to K = 10 lowers WCSS further but with diminishing returns (the elbow in the plot), and the visual gain is mostly smoother gradients and finer detail. K = 5 stores 5 colors instead of thousands, so it is a good compression/fidelity trade-off.

Question 3: Hierarchical clustering of cars

The file data/mtcars.csv contains 11 numerical variables for 32 cars, including fuel economy, horsepower, and weight. The car column gives the model names; use it to label observations, not as a clustering variable. You may use existing hierarchical clustering functions for this question.

  1. Standardize each numerical variable to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Using Euclidean distance, perform hierarchical clustering with single, complete, and average linkage. Plot the three dendrograms with the car names and compare the results.

  2. Choose one linkage method and a number of clusters that you consider reasonable. Report the cluster memberships and a table of cluster means on the original variable scales. Describe the main characteristics of the groups and explain your choice using the dendrogram and table. Briefly explain why standardizing the variables matters for this analysis.

Solution for Question 3

cars <- read.csv("data/mtcars.csv")
vars <- setdiff(names(cars), "car")
dim(cars); vars
[1] 32 12
 [1] "mpg"  "cyl"  "disp" "hp"   "drat" "wt"   "qsec" "vs"   "am"   "gear"
[11] "carb"
  1. Dendograms
Z <- scale(cars[, vars])                  
rownames(Z) <- cars$car
d <- dist(Z, method = "euclidean")

hcs <- lapply(c(single = "single", complete = "complete", average = "average"),
              function(m) hclust(d, method = m))

par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 3, 1))
for (m in names(hcs)) {
  plot(hcs[[m]], labels = cars$car, hang = -1, cex = 0.7, xlab = "", sub = "",
       main = paste(tools::toTitleCase(m), "linkage"))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
sapply(hcs, function(h) table(cutree(h, k = 4)))
  single complete average
1     18        5      11
2     12        8       7
3      1        7      12
4      1       12       2

Single linkage merges clusters by their nearest pair of members, so it produces the typical “chaining” pattern: a long staircase in which cars are added one at a time to a big cluster and a few outlying cars are left as singletons. This gives unbalanced, hard-to-interpret groups. Complete linkage uses the farthest pair, giving compact, more balanced clusters, and average linkage lies between the two. Complete and average linkage give similar, more interpretable structures, with the unusual cars joining late

  1. I choose complete linkage with K = 4 clusters. The dendrogram shows long vertical gaps before the last few merges, so cutting at 4 groups separates clearly distinct branches while still giving groups of reasonable size.
hc <- hcs$complete
grp <- cutree(hc, k = 4)

for (g in sort(unique(grp))) {
  cat("\nCluster", g, "(n =", sum(grp == g), "):\n")
  cat(paste(cars$car[grp == g], collapse = ", "), "\n")
}

plot(hc, labels = cars$car, hang = -1, cex = 0.7, xlab = "", sub = "",
     main = "Complete linkage, cut into 4 clusters")
rect.hclust(hc, k = 4, border = 2:5)

The table shows that the groups differ mainly along one size/power axis: cars with large displacement, many cylinders (8), high horsepower and high weight have low mpg, while small cars with 4 cylinders, low weight and displacement have high mpg. Intermediate 6-cylinder cars fall in between, and a small group of high-performance cars stands out through very high horsepower and carburetors, together with short quarter-mile times . Transmission and engine help distinguish the small economical cars from the heavy ones. I chose K = 4 because the dendrogram has large jumps in height there, and the cluster means in the table are meaningfully different on most variables, whereas larger K would split these groups into very small clusters.The variables are measured on very different scales. Euclidean distance is driven by the variables with the largest numeric variance, so without standardizing, disp and hp would dominate the clustering and the other variables would barely matter.
